procedural_history.originating_court: The case originated with a petition to the Supreme Court of India under Article 32 of the Constitution.
procedural_history.impugned_order: The petitioners challenged orders of detention passed under Section 3(2) of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: There were no High Court proceedings mentioned in the text. The case went directly to the Supreme Court under its original jurisdiction related to Article 32.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court issued a rule calling upon the State of West Bengal (the respondent) to show cause why a writ of habeas corpus should not be issued. The Court then considered the cases of the petitioners in three groups, ultimately granting the writ and ordering the release of some petitioners while rejecting the petitions of others.

directions: The order of detention made by the District Magistrate, Howrah under s. 3 (2) of the Act dated January 20, 1968 against petitioner Subhas Chandra Bose alias Kanta Bose and the consequent order made by the Governor dated March 30, 1968 confuming the order of detention under s. 11 ( l ) of the Act must be declared to be illegal.

issue.issue_text: Whether a detention order is rendered illegal if even one of the grounds provided to the detenu is found to be irrelevant or so vague that it prevents the detenu from making an effective representation.

facts: A detenu was served with an order of detention that listed multiple grounds.

The issue before the court was whether the entire detention order becomes illegal if just one of those grounds is found to be either irrelevant to the purpose of the detention act or so vague that it prevents the detenu from properly defending themselves.
law: The satisfaction of the detaining authority is subjective and generally not questionable in court.
However, the grounds for detention must be relevant and germane to the matters specified in the Preventive Detention Act.
Under Article 22(5) of the Constitution, the detenu has a right to be provided with the grounds for their detention and the earliest opportunity to make a representation against the order.

This constitutional requirement implies that the grounds must not be vague. A ground is considered vague if it is not definite enough to be intelligently understood and to furnish the detenu with sufficient material to make an effective representation.
application: The Court reasoned that if even one ground is irrelevant, the entire detention order is invalid. This is because it is impossible to know to what extent the 'bad reason' influenced the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority, or if the order would have been made at all based only on the valid grounds.

Similarly, if one ground is so vague that it deprives the detenu of their constitutional right to make an effective representation, the detention is not in accordance with the procedure established by law.

The Court held that the constitutional requirement that grounds not be vague must be satisfied for each individual ground. Therefore, even if other grounds are perfectly valid and clear, a single vague ground is sufficient to invalidate the entire detention order.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a detention order is rendered illegal if even one of the grounds provided is found to be irrelevant or so vague that it prevents the detenu from making an effective representation. The presence of a single invalid ground (whether irrelevant or vague) vitiates the entire order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the court can question the reasonableness of the detaining authority's satisfaction or the adequacy of the material on which the satisfaction is based.

law.fact: The satisfaction of the detaining authority required by the relevant statute (s. 3(1)(a)) is a subjective satisfaction.
law.source: It is well-settled that the satisfaction of the detaining authority • fo which s. 3 ( 1 )(a) refers is a subjective satisfaction, and so is G not justi<:iable.

law.fact: A subjective satisfaction is not justiciable, meaning it cannot be reviewed or questioned by a court on its merits.
law.source: The reasonableness of the satisfaction of the detaining autho- rity cannot be questioned in a Court of law; the adequacy of the mate-rial on which the said satisfaction purports to rest also cannot be examined in a Court of law.

law.fact: However, a detention order can be challenged and quashed on other grounds, such as mala fides (bad faith), the use of irrelevant grounds, or grounds that are so vague they prevent the detenu from making a representation.
law.source: But if any of the grounds furnished to the detenu are found to be irrelevant...the satisfaction of the detaining authority on which the order of detention is based is open to challenge... Similarly, if some of the grounds supplied to the detenu are so vague that they would virtually deprive the detenu of his statutory right of making a representation, that again may make the order of detention invalid.

application.fact: The Court established that since the authority's satisfaction is subjective, it is not open to the court to apply objective tests to determine if the satisfaction was justified.
application.source: Therefore it would not be open to the detenu •faction of the detainjng authority is not reasonably based on any of the said grounds.

application.fact: A detenu cannot argue that the grounds provided do not reasonably lead to the conclusion that they would engage in prejudicial activities if not detained.
application.source: It would not be open, for instance, to the detenu to contend that the grounds supplied to him do not necessarily or reasonably lead to the conclusion that if he is not detained, he would indulge in prejudicial activities.

application.fact: The Court clarified that the reasonableness of the authority's satisfaction can only be considered incidentally when a detenu challenges the detention on the grounds of mala fides (bad faith).
application.source: In support of the plea of ma/a fides the detenu may urge that along with other facts which show ma/a fides, the grounds served on him cannot ration- ally support the conclusion drawn against him by the detaining authority. It is only in this incidental manner that this question can become justiciable

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition, holding that the satisfaction of the detaining authority is subjective and therefore not justiciable. A court cannot question the reasonableness of this satisfaction or the adequacy of the material it is based on. The court's review is limited to procedural fairness and legality, such as whether the grounds are irrelevant, vague, or if the order was made in bad faith (mala fides).

issue.issue_text: Whether grounds of detention detailing assaults on solitary individuals have a relevant and proximate connection with the 'maintenance of public order'.

facts: The grounds for detention for some of the petitioners included several instances of assault on solitary individuals, committed either with a knife or by using crackers.
law: The Court drew a distinction between a 'law and order' issue and a 'public order' issue.
A contravention of law only affects 'public order' if it impacts the community or the public at large.
A line must be drawn between serious disorders that directly affect the community and minor, local breaches of peace that primarily injure specific individuals.

Acts that primarily injure specific persons and only secondarily affect the public interest are considered 'law and order' issues, not 'public order' issues, and are insufficient for action under the Preventive Detention Act.
application: The Court categorized the assaults on solitary individuals as acts that primarily injure specific persons.
It reasoned that while these acts are disturbances of 'law and order', they are of a purely local significance and do not rise to the level of affecting the community at large.
Therefore, the Court found it difficult to accept that these grounds had any relevant or proximate connection with the 'maintenance of public order'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that grounds of detention detailing assaults on solitary individuals do not have a relevant and proximate connection with the 'maintenance of public order'. Such acts are breaches of 'law and order' but do not affect the public at large, and therefore cannot be used to justify preventive detention.

issue.issue_text: Whether a ground for detention stating that the petitioner has 'become a menace to the society' and that inhabitants are in 'constant dread of disturbances of public order' is unconstitutionally vague.

facts: A petitioner was detained on grounds that included the statement: "You have become a menace to the society and there have been disturbances and confusion in the lives of peaceful citizens of Baraset and Khardah P.S. areas under 24-Parganas District and the inhabitants thereof are in constant dread of disturbances of public order."
law: The Court relied on the constitutional safeguard provided under Article 22(5), which requires that a detained person must be provided with grounds for detention that are specific enough to enable them to make an adequate representation against it.
A ground is considered 'vague' if it is incapable of being understood or defined with sufficient certainty, preventing the detained person from properly meeting the charge.

The Court also cited the principle that if even one of the grounds for detention is found to be vague, the entire detention order is illegal, as it's impossible to know to what extent the invalid ground influenced the detaining authority's decision.
application: The Court examined the specific wording of the ground and found it to be "extremely vague."
It reasoned that the statement gave no specific particulars or details about the petitioner's alleged actions.
Without these particulars, the petitioner could not formulate an adequate or intelligent representation to defend themselves against the detention order, thus violating their constitutional right.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the ground for detention was unconstitutionally vague because it lacked the necessary particulars to allow the petitioner to make an adequate representation. This vagueness infringed the constitutional safeguard under Article 22(5), rendering the detention order illegal and ultra vires.

cases.principle: If an order of detention is based on both a valid and an invalid ground, the entire order must be held to be illegal because it cannot be determined in what manner and to what extent the valid and invalid grounds operated on the mind of the authority and contributed to their subjective satisfaction.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An order of detention is invalid if any of the grounds that led to the detaining authority's satisfaction are found to be irrelevant or foreign to the authorizing statute, even if other valid grounds exist. This is because it is impossible to determine to what extent the invalid ground influenced the authority's decision. Similarly, an order of detention is invalid if some of the grounds provided are so vague that they effectively deprive the detainee of their statutory right to make a representation.
obiter: If the grounds for an order of detention are relevant and germane to the matters considered under the statute, a court cannot challenge the order by arguing that the detaining authority's satisfaction was not reasonably based on those grounds.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the detention order was illegal because several of the grounds provided, specifically those relating to assaults on solitary individuals, had no relevant or proximate connection to the 'maintenance of public order'. The established legal principle is that if even one of the grounds relied upon by the detaining authority is irrelevant or invalid, the entire detention order must be struck down. This is because it is impossible for a court to determine to what extent the invalid ground influenced the authority's subjective satisfaction, or whether the order would have been made at all based solely on the valid grounds.
legal_tests_applied: The 'one bad ground' test: Even if any one of the grounds or reasons that led to the satisfaction is irrelevant, the order of detention would be invalid even if there were other relevant grounds, because it can never be certain to what extent the bad reasons operated on the mind of the authority concerned.

The 'vagueness' test: If some of the grounds supplied to the detenu are so vague that they would virtually deprive the detenu of his statutory right of making a representation, that may make the order of detention invalid.

The 'subjective satisfaction' doctrine: The satisfaction of the detaining authority is a subjective satisfaction and is not justiciable. The reasonableness of the satisfaction and the adequacy of the material on which it rests cannot be questioned in a Court of law.
The 'relevance and proximate connection' test: Grounds for detention must have a relevant and proximate connection with the statutory purpose, such as the maintenance of public order.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the court should be able to question the reasonableness of the detaining authority's satisfaction was rejected. The court held that the satisfaction of the detaining authority is subjective and not justiciable, and it is not open to the detenu to contend that the grounds do not reasonably lead to the authority's conclusion.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that the court cannot question the reasonableness of the detaining authority's satisfaction or the adequacy of the material on which it is based. The court affirmed that this satisfaction is subjective and not open to objective tests in a court of law.
policy_considerations: To protect the statutory right of a detenu to make an effective representation, the grounds provided must not be so vague as to render this right meaningless.

To safeguard personal liberty against executive action, if a detention order is based on multiple grounds, the invalidity of even one ground is fatal to the entire order. This is because it is impossible to sever the good grounds from the bad and speculate on what the detaining authority would have done if only presented with the valid grounds.
